rationale: A wins because it turns the launch into four separable reported stories and puts a verification spine under each. Its installer angle, "The installer bottleneck: a home battery that claims it skips the rewiring," names the sharpest claim and the exact people who can kill or validate it. B has good bones, especially "Anker says its home battery skips the rewiring - installers will decide if that's true," but it is thinner and lets invented color like "brand known for $20 chargers" slip into the deck. That is not fatal, but it is how sloppy pitches learn to walk upright.
gaps_in_A: "who is allowed to sell into the home electrical panel" overreaches a bit; the update gives a category move, not evidence of regulatory or channel permission dynamics.
"when a competing product is actually on sale in the US, which is now" may overstate the launch; the update says launching, while orderability is still an unanswered question.
"any comment from a competitor" is nice-to-have proof, not core proof; price, usable capacity, warranty, availability, and installed cost are the meat.
The customer angle is useful but not pitch-ready without "at least one real US household"; A admits that, but it still makes the set partly dependent on proof Anker has not supplied.
gaps_in_B: "brand known for $20 chargers" invents a price point. The update says phone chargers and power banks, not twenty-dollar anything.
"a purchase measured in thousands of dollars and decades on the wall" may be category-common, but it is not in the update and warranty terms are explicitly not detailed.
It misses the homeowner economics angle even though "run a home during outages and cut peak-rate bills" is the clearest reader-facing fact in the brief.

The Powerwall proof list is undercooked: it asks for a spokesperson to address Tesla, but omits warranty terms, installer coverage, usable capacity comparison, and installed all-in cost. Those are the teeth.
